title: Oklahoma Oil Company Plugs Disposal Well That Posed Threat to City’s Drinking Water
author: Nick Bowlin
content:
An Oklahoma oil and gas company plugged a well that disposes of oil
production’s toxic byproduct after an [investigation by The Frontier and
ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org/article/enid-oklahoma-oil-gas-
pollution-water-protections) revealed that regulators had approved the well in
violation of state rules meant to protect public groundwater supplies.

The disposal well, named the Flying Monkey, injected oil field wastewater
underground and sat roughly a quarter-mile from two municipal groundwater
supply sites that served the small city of Enid in northwest Oklahoma.
Wastewater injection operations are banned within a half-mile of public water
wells unless regulators hold a hearing to ensure that this activity will not
pollute groundwater. Regulators at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission did not
hold a hearing before approving the well in 2018.

The city of Enid filed a complaint last year asking the state to revoke the
Flying Monkey’s permit to operate.

On Sept. 14, with the complaint still active in the agency’s administrative
law court, employees of the Flying Monkey’s current owner — BCE-Mach III
Midstream Holdings LLC — dropped a cast iron plug into the bottom of the well,
followed by more than 200 sacks of cement, to permanently seal it off,
according to a report the company filed to the corporation commission. A
representative of the state was on site to witness the plugging.

Eric Huddleston, an attorney representing BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings,
which acquired the Flying Monkey in 2020, said the company decided to
permanently shut the well after determining it was “underutilized and
operationally unnecessary.” A spokesperson for the corporation commission did
not respond to requests for comment, including about the agency’s role in the
well’s closure.

Enid city officials said they did not know the well had been plugged until our
reporter informed them.

“This decision is, for lack of a better word, thrilling because this is such a
vital issue,” said Frank Baker, an Enid city commissioner. “Our water sources
have been put in danger, and for this one well to have been plugged, this is
the best possible outcome.”

In Enid’s 2025 complaint to the state, its lawyers noted that the Flying
Monkey’s original operator, Hinkle Oil & Gas, had incorrectly checked a box on
its permit application stating that the injection well was not within a half-
mile of a public water supply well. “This was demonstrably false,” Enid’s
lawyers wrote. Hinkle previously declined to answer questions about the Flying
Monkey. Earlier this year, BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings refiled a permit
application for the Flying Monkey, where it acknowledged the proximity of the
city’s water supply wells.

![A small beige building with an antenna in a dry, grassy field. Power lines,
a wind turbine and a set of brown structures are
nearby.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/CEM_2779_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)A
building containing one of Enid’s groundwater supply wells sits about a
quarter-mile from the now-plugged Flying Monkey disposal well. September Dawn
Bottoms for ProPublica

The Flying Monkey had a checkered operational history. In the last five years,
the state has shut down the wastewater disposal well repeatedly after it
failed tests of its structural integrity. These failures can indicate a
problem that might allow wastewater to escape, potentially threatening
drinking water sources. The well had failed five of these tests since 2021.

In early July, nine days after the newsrooms’ investigation published, the
Flying Monkey’s owner reported another leak in the well’s tubing. The state
gave BCE-Mach III Midstream Holdings 90 days to fix the leak or to permanently
plug the well.

Our investigation identified two other wells in Enid that violated the state
distance rule between wastewater injection wells and the city’s groundwater
supply sites. Both of those wells, which are owned by other companies, remain
active.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/20260427-Bottoms-
OKEnidChallenge_2752_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **To
Protect Its Drinking Water, This City Has to Appeal to the Oil Regulators That
Put It at Risk** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/enid-oklahoma-oil-gas-
pollution-water-protections)

The proximity of wells to drinking water isn’t only an issue in Enid. Across
Oklahoma, the news outlets identified at least 114 injection wells that were
located within a half-mile of a public water supply well. More than 300,000
Oklahomans live in communities that rely on these water wells, according to
our analysis.

Baker, the Enid official, told The Frontier and ProPublica that he hopes the
corporation commission will begin to plug other injection wells that threaten
public water supplies.

“I hope and pray this is an example that we’ll start to see replicated across
the state in the near future,” he said.

In addition to its request to plug the well, the city of Enid has asked the
corporation commission to impose stronger regulations on oilfield wastewater
disposal near its water supply, including a wider distance buffer between the
injection sites and the city’s water wells. This request comes amid a recent
uptick in wastewater injection in the Enid area, according to a legal filing
made by the city. The commission previously declined to comment on Enid’s
complaint because it is an active case. The case will continue to be heard in
the agency’s administrative law court later this year.

Drinking Water](https://www.propublica.org/article/enid-oklahoma-oil-disposal-
